[54](#54)pub fn find_executable(name: &str) -> Option<PathBuf> {
[55](#55)    static CACHE: Lazy<RwLock<FxHashMap<String, PathBuf>>> = Lazy::new(Default::default);
[56](#56)
[57](#57)    {
[58](#58)        let locked = CACHE.read().unwrap();
[59](#59)        if let Some(cached) = locked.get(name) {
[60](#60)            return Some(cached.clone());
[61](#61)        }
[62](#62)    }
[63](#63)
[64](#64)    let mut path = env::var_os("PATH").and_then(|paths| {
[65](#65)        env::split_paths(&paths)
[66](#66)            .filter_map(|dir| {
[67](#67)                let full_path = dir.join(name);
[68](#68)                if full_path.is_file() {
[69](#69)                    Some(full_path)
[70](#70)                } else {
[71](#71)                    None
[72](#72)                }
[73](#73)            })
[74](#74)            .next()
[75](#75)    });
[76](#76)
[77](#77)    if path.is_none() {
[78](#78)        path = Command::new("yarn")
[81](#81)            .arg("bin")
[82](#82)            .arg(name)
[83](#83)            .output()
[84](#84)            .ok()
[85](#85)            .and_then(|output| {
[86](#86)                if output.status.success() {
[87](#87)                    let path = String::from_utf8(output.stdout).ok()?;
[88](#88)                    let path = path.trim();
[89](#89)                    let path = PathBuf::from(path);
[90](#90)                    if path.is_file() {
[91](#91)                        return Some(path);
[92](#92)                    }
[93](#93)                }
[94](#94)
[95](#95)                None
[96](#96)            });
[97](#97)    }
[98](#98)
[99](#99)    if let Some(path) = path.clone() {
[100](#100)        let mut locked = CACHE.write().unwrap();
[101](#101)        locked.insert(name.to_string(), path);
[102](#102)    }

[183](#183)    where
[184](#184)        F: FnOnce(Lrc<SourceMap>, Handler) -> Result<Ret, ()>,
[185](#185)    {

[189](#189)            self::diag_errors::new_handler(self.cm.clone(), self.treat_err_as_bug);

[191](#191)
[192](#192)        let mut errs: Vec<_> = errors.into();
[193](#193)        errs.sort_by_key(|d| {
[194](#194)            let span = d.span.primary_span().unwrap();
[195](#195)            let cp = self.cm.lookup_char_pos(span.lo());
[196](#196)
[197](#197)            let line = cp.line;
[198](#198)            let column = cp.col.0 + 1;
[199](#199)
[200](#200)            line * 10000 + column
[201](#201)        });
[202](#202)
[203](#203)        match result {
[204](#204)            Ok(res) => Ok(res),
[205](#205)            Err(()) => Err(errs),
[206](#206)        }
[207](#207)    }

[223](#223)pub fn print_left_right(left: &dyn Debug, right: &dyn Debug) -> String {
[224](#224)    fn print(t: &dyn Debug) -> String {
[225](#225)        let s = format!("{t:#?}");
[226](#226)
[227](#227)        let s = {
[229](#229)            static RE: Lazy<Regex> =
[230](#230)                Lazy::new(|| Regex::new("Span \\{[\\a-zA-Z0#:\\(\\)]*\\}").unwrap());
[231](#231)
[232](#232)            &RE
[233](#233)        }
[234](#234)        .replace_all(&s, "_");
[235](#235)        let s = {
[237](#237)            static RE: Lazy<Regex> = Lazy::new(|| Regex::new("span: _[,]?\\s*").unwrap());
[238](#238)
[239](#239)            &RE
[240](#240)        }
[241](#241)        .replace_all(&s, "");
[242](#242)
[243](#243)        s.into()
[244](#244)    }
[245](#245)
[246](#246)    let (left, right) = (print(left), print(right));
[247](#247)
[248](#248)    let cur = thread::current();
[249](#249)    let test_name = cur
[250](#250)        .name()
[251](#251)        .expect("rustc sets test name as the name of thread");
[252](#252)
[253](#253)    let target_dir = {
[255](#255)        let mut buf = paths::test_results_dir().to_path_buf();
[256](#256)        for m in test_name.split("::") {
[257](#257)            buf.push(m)
[258](#258)        }
[259](#259)
[260](#260)        create_dir_all(&buf).unwrap_or_else(|err| {
[261](#261)            panic!(
[262](#262)                "failed to create directory ({}) for writing data of the failed assertion: {}",
[263](#263)                buf.display(),
[264](#264)                err
[265](#265)            )
[266](#266)        });
[267](#267)
[268](#268)        buf
[269](#269)    };
[270](#270)
[271](#271)    write_to_file(&target_dir.join("left"), &left);
[272](#272)    write_to_file(&target_dir.join("right"), &right);
[273](#273)
[274](#274)    format!("----- {test_name}\n    left:\n{left}\n    right:\n{right}")
[275](#275)}

[306](#306)pub fn unignore_fixture(fixture_path: &Path) {
[308](#308)    if fixture_path.components().all(|c| {
[309](#309)        !matches!(c, Component::Normal(..)) || !c.as_os_str().to_string_lossy().starts_with('.')
[310](#310)    }) {
[311](#311)        return;
[312](#312)    }
[313](#313)    let mut new_path = PathBuf::new();
[316](#316)
[317](#317)    for c in fixture_path.components() {
[318](#318)        if let Component::Normal(s) = c {
[319](#319)            if let Some(s) = s.to_string_lossy().strip_prefix('.') {
[320](#320)                new_path.push(s);
[321](#321)
[322](#322)                continue;
[323](#323)            }
[324](#324)        }
[325](#325)        new_path.push(c);
[326](#326)    }
[327](#327)
[328](#328)    create_dir_all(new_path.parent().unwrap()).expect("failed to create parent dir");
[329](#329)
[330](#330)    rename(fixture_path, &new_path).expect("failed to rename");
[331](#331)}

# assert_eq in testing - Rust

Source: https://rustdoc.swc.rs/testing/macro.assert_eq.html

# Macro assert_eq

```
macro_rules! assert_eq {
    ($left:expr, $right:expr$(,)?) => { ... };
    ($left:expr, $right:expr, $($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
    (@ $left:expr, $right:expr, $maybe_colon:expr, $($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using [ PartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialEq.html)).

On panic, this macro will print a diff derived from [ Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) representation of
each value.

This is a drop in replacement for [ core::assert_eq!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.assert_eq.html).
You can provide a custom panic message if desired.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples)Examples

```
use pretty_assertions::assert_eq;
let a = 3;
let b = 1 + 2;
assert_eq!(a, b);
assert_eq!(a, b, "we are testing addition with {} and {}", a, b);
```

---

# assert_ne in testing - Rust

Source: https://rustdoc.swc.rs/testing/macro.assert_ne.html

# Macro assert_ne

```
macro_rules! assert_ne {
    ($left:expr, $right:expr$(,)?) => { ... };
    ($left:expr, $right:expr, $($arg:tt)+) => { ... };
    (@ $left:expr, $right:expr, $maybe_colon:expr, $($arg:tt)+) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Asserts that two expressions are not equal to each other (using [ PartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialEq.html)).

On panic, this macro will print the values of the expressions with their
[ Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) representations.

This is a drop in replacement for [ core::assert_ne!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.assert_ne.html).
You can provide a custom panic message if desired.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples)Examples

```
use pretty_assertions::assert_ne;
let a = 3;
let b = 2;
assert_ne!(a, b);
assert_ne!(a, b, "we are testing that the values are not equal");
```

---

# NormalizedOutput in testing - Rust

Source: https://rustdoc.swc.rs/testing/struct.NormalizedOutput.html

`pub struct NormalizedOutput(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

Normalized stdout/stderr.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#normalization)Normalization

See https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/b224fc84e3/src/test/COMPILER_TESTS.md#normalization

-
The `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`directory is replaced with`$DIR`.
-
All backslashes () within same line as `$DIR`are converted to forward slashes (/) (for Windows) - All CR LF newlines are converted to LF
-
`normalize-stdout`is not implemented (yet?).

## Implementations[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#implementations)

1.9.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#360)#### pub fn [is_char_boundary](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.is_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#360)

#### pub fn [is_char_boundary](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.is_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Checks that `index`-th byte is the first byte in a UTF-8 code point
sequence or the end of the string.

The start and end of the string (when `index == self.len()`) are
considered to be boundaries.

Returns `false` if `index` is greater than `self.len()`.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard";
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(0));
// start of `老`
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(6));
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(s.len()));
// second byte of `ö`
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(2));
// third byte of `老`
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(8));
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#409)#### pub fn [floor_char_boundary](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.floor_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

`round_char_boundary`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#409)

#### pub fn [floor_char_boundary](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.floor_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

`round_char_boundary`)Finds the closest `x` not exceeding `index` where [ is_char_boundary(x)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.is_char_boundary) is

`true`.This method can help you truncate a string so that it’s still valid UTF-8, but doesn’t exceed a given number of bytes. Note that this is done purely at the character level and can still visually split graphemes, even though the underlying characters aren’t split. For example, the emoji 🧑🔬 (scientist) could be split so that the string only includes 🧑 (person) instead.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
#![feature(round_char_boundary)]
let s = "❤️🧡💛💚💙💜";
assert_eq!(s.len(), 26);
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(13));
let closest = s.floor_char_boundary(13);
assert_eq!(closest, 10);
assert_eq!(&s[..closest], "❤️🧡");
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#447)#### pub fn [ceil_char_boundary](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.ceil_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

`round_char_boundary`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#447)

#### pub fn [ceil_char_boundary](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.ceil_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

`round_char_boundary`)Finds the closest `x` not below `index` where [ is_char_boundary(x)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.is_char_boundary) is

`true`.If `index` is greater than the length of the string, this returns the length of the string.

This method is the natural complement to [ floor_char_boundary](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.floor_char_boundary). See that method
for more details.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
#![feature(round_char_boundary)]
let s = "❤️🧡💛💚💙💜";
assert_eq!(s.len(), 26);
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(13));
let closest = s.ceil_char_boundary(13);
assert_eq!(closest, 14);
assert_eq!(&s[..closest], "❤️🧡💛");
```
Converts a string slice to a raw pointer.

As string slices are a slice of bytes, the raw pointer points to a
[ u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html). This pointer will be pointing to the first byte of the string
slice.

The caller must ensure that the returned pointer is never written to.
If you need to mutate the contents of the string slice, use [ as_mut_ptr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.as_mut_ptr).

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
let s = "Hello";
let ptr = s.as_ptr();
```
Returns a subslice of `str`.

This is the non-panicking alternative to indexing the `str`. Returns
[ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) whenever equivalent indexing operation would panic.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
let v = String::from("🗻∈🌏");
assert_eq!(Some("🗻"), v.get(0..4));
// indices not on UTF-8 sequence boundaries
assert!(v.get(1..).is_none());
assert!(v.get(..8).is_none());
// out of bounds
assert!(v.get(..42).is_none());
```
1.20.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#656)#### pub unsafe fn [get_unchecked](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.get_unchecked)<I>(&self, i: I) -> &<I as [SliceIndex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html)<[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)>>::[Output](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html#associatedtype.Output)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#656)

#### pub unsafe fn [get_unchecked](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.get_unchecked)<I>(&self, i: I) -> &<I as [SliceIndex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html)<[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)>>::[Output](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html#associatedtype.Output)

Returns an unchecked subslice of `str`.

This is the unchecked alternative to indexing the `str`.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#safety)Safety

Callers of this function are responsible that these preconditions are satisfied:

- The starting index must not exceed the ending index;
- Indexes must be within bounds of the original slice;
- Indexes must lie on UTF-8 sequence boundaries.

Failing that, the returned string slice may reference invalid memory or
violate the invariants communicated by the `str` type.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
let v = "🗻∈🌏";
unsafe {
    assert_eq!("🗻", v.get_unchecked(0..4));
    assert_eq!("∈", v.get_unchecked(4..7));
    assert_eq!("🌏", v.get_unchecked(7..11));
}
```

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#742)

#### pub unsafe fn [slice_unchecked](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.slice_unchecked)(&self, begin: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), end: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

`get_unchecked(begin..end)` insteadCreates a string slice from another string slice, bypassing safety checks.

This is generally not recommended, use with caution! For a safe
alternative see [ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/index/trait.Index.html)

`Index`This new slice goes from `begin` to `end`, including `begin` but
excluding `end`.

To get a mutable string slice instead, see the
[ slice_mut_unchecked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.slice_mut_unchecked) method.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#safety-1)Safety

Callers of this function are responsible that three preconditions are satisfied:

- `begin`must not exceed- `end`.
- `begin`and- `end`must be byte positions within the string slice.
- `begin`and- `end`must lie on UTF-8 sequence boundaries.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-9)Examples

    assert_eq!("world", s.slice_unchecked(7, 12));
}
```
Divides one string slice into two at an index.

The argument, `mid`, should be a byte offset from the start of the
string. It must also be on the boundary of a UTF-8 code point.

The two slices returned go from the start of the string slice to `mid`,
and from `mid` to the end of the string slice.

To get mutable string slices instead, see the [ split_at_mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_at_mut)
method.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if `mid` is not on a UTF-8 code point boundary, or if it is past
the end of the last code point of the string slice.  For a non-panicking
alternative see [ split_at_checked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_at_checked).

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
let s = "Per Martin-Löf";
let (first, last) = s.split_at(3);
assert_eq!("Per", first);
assert_eq!(" Martin-Löf", last);
```
Divides one string slice into two at an index.

The argument, `mid`, should be a valid byte offset from the start of the
string. It must also be on the boundary of a UTF-8 code point. The
method returns `None` if that’s not the case.

The two slices returned go from the start of the string slice to `mid`,
and from `mid` to the end of the string slice.

To get mutable string slices instead, see the [ split_at_mut_checked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_at_mut_checked)
method.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
let s = "Per Martin-Löf";
let (first, last) = s.split_at_checked(3).unwrap();
assert_eq!("Per", first);
assert_eq!(" Martin-Löf", last);
assert_eq!(None, s.split_at_checked(13));  // Inside “ö”
assert_eq!(None, s.split_at_checked(16));  // Beyond the string length
```
Returns an iterator over the [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s of a string slice.

As a string slice consists of valid UTF-8, we can iterate through a
string slice by [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html). This method returns such an iterator.

It’s important to remember that [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html) represents a Unicode Scalar
Value, and might not match your idea of what a ‘character’ is. Iteration
over grapheme clusters may be what you actually want. This functionality
is not provided by Rust’s standard library, check crates.io instead.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-12)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let word = "goodbye";
let count = word.chars().count();
assert_eq!(7, count);
let mut chars = word.chars();
assert_eq!(Some('g'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('o'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('o'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('d'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('b'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('y'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('e'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(None, chars.next());
```
Remember, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s might not match your intuition about characters:

```
let y = "y̆";
let mut chars = y.chars();
assert_eq!(Some('y'), chars.next()); // not 'y̆'
assert_eq!(Some('\u{0306}'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(None, chars.next());
```

#### pub fn [char_indices](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.char_indices)(&self) -> [CharIndices](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.CharIndices.html)<'_>

Returns an iterator over the [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s of a string slice, and their

As a string slice consists of valid UTF-8, we can iterate through a
string slice by [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html). This method returns an iterator of both
these

[s, as well as their byte positions.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`The iterator yields tuples. The position is first, the [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html) is
second.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-13)Examples

Basic usage:

```

assert_eq!(Some((4, 'b')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(Some((5, 'y')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(Some((6, 'e')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(None, char_indices.next());
```
Remember, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s might not match your intuition about characters:

```
let yes = "y̆es";
let mut char_indices = yes.char_indices();
assert_eq!(Some((0, 'y')), char_indices.next()); // not (0, 'y̆')
assert_eq!(Some((1, '\u{0306}')), char_indices.next());
// note the 3 here - the previous character took up two bytes
assert_eq!(Some((3, 'e')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(Some((4, 's')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(None, char_indices.next());
```
Returns an iterator over the bytes of a string slice.

As a string slice consists of a sequence of bytes, we can iterate through a string slice by byte. This method returns such an iterator.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-14)Examples

1.1.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1166)#### pub fn [split_whitespace](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.split_whitespace)(&self) -> [SplitWhitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitWhitespace.html)<'_>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1166)

#### pub fn [split_whitespace](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.split_whitespace)(&self) -> [SplitWhitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitWhitespace.html)<'_>

Splits a string slice by whitespace.

The iterator returned will return string slices that are sub-slices of the original string slice, separated by any amount of whitespace.

‘Whitespace’ is defined according to the terms of the Unicode Derived
Core Property `White_Space`. If you only want to split on ASCII whitespace
instead, use [ split_ascii_whitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_ascii_whitespace).

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-15)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let mut iter = "A few words".split_whitespace();
assert_eq!(Some("A"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("few"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("words"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(None, iter.next());
```
All kinds of whitespace are considered:

```
let mut iter = " Mary   had\ta\u{2009}little  \n\t lamb".split_whitespace();
assert_eq!(Some("Mary"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("had"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("a"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("little"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("lamb"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(None, iter.next());
```
If the string is empty or all whitespace, the iterator yields no string slices:

```
assert_eq!("".split_whitespace().next(), None);
assert_eq!("   ".split_whitespace().next(), None);
```

Returns an iterator over the lines of a string, as string slices.

Lines are split at line endings that are either newlines (`\n`) or
sequences of a carriage return followed by a line feed (`\r\n`).

Line terminators are not included in the lines returned by the iterator.

Note that any carriage return (`\r`) not immediately followed by a
line feed (`\n`) does not split a line. These carriage returns are
thereby included in the produced lines.

The final line ending is optional. A string that ends with a final line ending will return the same lines as an otherwise identical string without a final line ending.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-17)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let text = "foo\r\nbar\n\nbaz\r";
let mut lines = text.lines();
assert_eq!(Some("foo"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some("bar"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some(""), lines.next());
// Trailing carriage return is included in the last line
assert_eq!(Some("baz\r"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(None, lines.next());
```
The final line does not require any ending:

```
let text = "foo\nbar\n\r\nbaz";
let mut lines = text.lines();
assert_eq!(Some("foo"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some("bar"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some(""), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some("baz"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(None, lines.next());
```
1.0.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1277) 👎Deprecated since 1.4.0: use lines() instead now

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1277)

Returns an iterator over the lines of a string.

1.0.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1360)#### pub fn [starts_with](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.starts_with)<P>(&self, pat: P) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

#### pub fn [starts_with](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.starts_with)<P>(&self, pat: P) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns `true` if the given pattern matches a prefix of this
string slice.

Returns `false` if it does not.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, in which case this function will return true if
the `&str` is a prefix of this string slice.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can also be a [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches. These will only be checked against the first character of this string slice. Look at the second example below regarding behavior for slices of](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[s.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

assert!(!bananas.starts_with("nana"));
```
```
let bananas = "bananas";
// Note that both of these assert successfully.
assert!(bananas.starts_with(&['b', 'a', 'n', 'a']));
assert!(bananas.starts_with(&['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']));
```

Returns `false` if it does not.

Returns the byte index of the first character of this string slice that matches the pattern.

Returns [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if the pattern doesn’t match.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-22)Examples

Simple patterns:

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard Gepardi";
assert_eq!(s.find('L'), Some(0));
assert_eq!(s.find('é'), Some(14));
assert_eq!(s.find("pard"), Some(17));
```
More complex patterns using point-free style and closures:

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard";
assert_eq!(s.find(char::is_whitespace), Some(5));
assert_eq!(s.find(char::is_lowercase), Some(1));
assert_eq!(s.find(|c: char| c.is_whitespace() || c.is_lowercase()), Some(1));
assert_eq!(s.find(|c: char| (c < 'o') && (c > 'a')), Some(4));
```
Not finding the pattern:

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard";
let x: &[_] = &['1', '2'];
assert_eq!(s.find(x), None);
```
Returns the byte index for the first character of the last match of the pattern in this string slice.

Returns [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if the pattern doesn’t match.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-23)Examples

Simple patterns:

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard Gepardi";
assert_eq!(s.rfind('L'), Some(13));
assert_eq!(s.rfind('é'), Some(14));
assert_eq!(s.rfind("pard"), Some(24));
```
More complex patterns with closures:

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard";
assert_eq!(s.rfind(char::is_whitespace), Some(12));
assert_eq!(s.rfind(char::is_lowercase), Some(20));
```
Not finding the pattern:

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard";
let x: &[_] = &['1', '2'];
assert_eq!(s.rfind(x), None);
```
Returns an iterator over substrings of this string slice, separated by characters matched by a pattern.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#iterator-behavior)Iterator behavior

The returned iterator will be a [ DoubleEndedIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/double_ended/trait.DoubleEndedIterator.html) if the pattern
allows a reverse search and forward/reverse search yields the same
elements. This is true for, e.g.,

[, but not for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char``&str`.If the pattern allows a reverse search but its results might differ
from a forward search, the [ rsplit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.rsplit) method can be used.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-24)Examples

Simple patterns:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lamb".split(' ').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["Mary", "had", "a", "little", "lamb"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "".split('X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, [""]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lionXXtigerXleopard".split('X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lion", "", "tiger", "leopard"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lion::tiger::leopard".split("::").collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lion", "tiger", "leopard"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "abc1def2ghi".split(char::is_numeric).collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["abc", "def", "ghi"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lionXtigerXleopard".split(char::is_uppercase).collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lion", "tiger", "leopard"]);
```
If the pattern is a slice of chars, split on each occurrence of any of the characters:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "2020-11-03 23:59".split(&['-', ' ', ':', '@'][..]).collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["2020", "11", "03", "23", "59"]);
```
A more complex pattern, using a closure:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "abc1defXghi".split(|c| c == '1' || c == 'X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["abc", "def", "ghi"]);
```
If a string contains multiple contiguous separators, you will end up with empty strings in the output:

```
let x = "||||a||b|c".to_string();
let d: Vec<_> = x.split('|').collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["", "", "", "", "a", "", "b", "c"]);
```
Contiguous separators are separated by the empty string.

```
let x = "(///)".to_string();
let d: Vec<_> = x.split('/').collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["(", "", "", ")"]);
```
Separators at the start or end of a string are neighbored by empty strings.

```
let d: Vec<_> = "010".split("0").collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["", "1", ""]);
```
When the empty string is used as a separator, it separates every character in the string, along with the beginning and end of the string.

```
let f: Vec<_> = "rust".split("").collect();
assert_eq!(f, &["", "r", "u", "s", "t", ""]);
```
Contiguous separators can lead to possibly surprising behavior when whitespace is used as the separator. This code is correct:

```
let x = "    a  b c".to_string();
let d: Vec<_> = x.split(' ').collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["", "", "", "", "a", "", "b", "c"]);
```
It does *not* give you:

Use [ split_whitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_whitespace) for this behavior.

1.51.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1645)#### pub fn [split_inclusive](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.split_inclusive)<P>(&self, pat: P) -> [SplitInclusive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitInclusive.html)<'_, P>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1645)

#### pub fn [split_inclusive](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.split_inclusive)<P>(&self, pat: P) -> [SplitInclusive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitInclusive.html)<'_, P>

Returns an iterator over substrings of this string slice, separated by characters matched by a pattern.

Differs from the iterator produced by `split` in that `split_inclusive`
leaves the matched part as the terminator of the substring.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-25)Examples

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lamb\nlittle lamb\nlittle lamb."
    .split_inclusive('\n').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["Mary had a little lamb\n", "little lamb\n", "little lamb."]);
```
If the last element of the string is matched, that element will be considered the terminator of the preceding substring. That substring will be the last item returned by the iterator.

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lamb\nlittle lamb\nlittle lamb.\n"
    .split_inclusive('\n').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["Mary had a little lamb\n", "little lamb\n", "little lamb.\n"]);
```
Returns an iterator over substrings of the given string slice, separated by characters matched by a pattern and yielded in reverse order.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#iterator-behavior-1)Iterator behavior

The returned iterator requires that the pattern supports a reverse
search, and it will be a [ DoubleEndedIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/double_ended/trait.DoubleEndedIterator.html) if a forward/reverse
search yields the same elements.

For iterating from the front, the [ split](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split) method can be used.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-26)Examples

Simple patterns:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lamb".rsplit(' ').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lamb", "little", "a", "had", "Mary"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "".rsplit('X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, [""]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lionXXtigerXleopard".rsplit('X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["leopard", "tiger", "", "lion"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lion::tiger::leopard".rsplit("::").collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["leopard", "tiger", "lion"]);
```
A more complex pattern, using a closure:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "abc1defXghi".rsplit(|c| c == '1' || c == 'X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["ghi", "def", "abc"]);
```

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`Equivalent to [ split](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split), except that the trailing substring is
skipped if empty.

This method can be used for string data that is *terminated*,
rather than *separated* by a pattern.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#iterator-behavior-3)Iterator behavior

The returned iterator requires that the pattern supports a reverse search, and it will be double ended if a forward/reverse search yields the same elements.

For iterating from the front, the [ split_terminator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_terminator) method can be

Returns an iterator over substrings of the given string slice, separated
by a pattern, restricted to returning at most `n` items.

If `n` substrings are returned, the last substring (the `n`th substring)
will contain the remainder of the string.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#iterator-behavior-4)Iterator behavior

The returned iterator will not be double ended, because it is not efficient to support.

If the pattern allows a reverse search, the [ rsplitn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.rsplitn) method can be
used.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-29)Examples

Simple patterns:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lambda".splitn(3, ' ').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["Mary", "had", "a little lambda"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lionXXtigerXleopard".splitn(3, "X").collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lion", "", "tigerXleopard"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "abcXdef".splitn(1, 'X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["abcXdef"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "".splitn(1, 'X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, [""]);
```
A more complex pattern, using a closure:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "abc1defXghi".splitn(2, |c| c == '1' || c == 'X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["abc", "defXghi"]);
```
Returns an iterator over substrings of this string slice, separated by a
pattern, starting from the end of the string, restricted to returning at
most `n` items.

If `n` substrings are returned, the last substring (the `n`th substring)
will contain the remainder of the string.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#iterator-behavior-5)Iterator behavior

The returned iterator will not be double ended, because it is not efficient to support.

For splitting from the front, the [ splitn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.splitn) method can be used.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-30)Examples

Simple patterns:

```

assert_eq!(v, ["lamb", "little", "Mary had a"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lionXXtigerXleopard".rsplitn(3, 'X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["leopard", "tiger", "lionX"]);

assert_eq!(v, ["leopard", "lion::tiger"]);

1.30.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#2158)#### pub fn [trim_start](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.trim_start)(&self) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#2158)

#### pub fn [trim_start](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.trim_start)(&self) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

Returns a string slice with leading whitespace removed.

‘Whitespace’ is defined according to the terms of the Unicode Derived
Core Property `White_Space`, which includes newlines.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#text-directionality)Text directionality

A string is a sequence of bytes. `start` in this context means the first
position of that byte string; for a left-to-right language like English or
Russian, this will be left side, and for right-to-left languages like
Arabic or Hebrew, this will be the right side.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-38)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let s = "\n Hello\tworld\t\n";
assert_eq!("Hello\tworld\t\n", s.trim_start());
```
Directionality:

```
let s = "  English  ";
assert!(Some('E') == s.trim_start().chars().next());
let s = "  עברית  ";
assert!(Some('ע') == s.trim_start().chars().next());
```
Returns a string slice with trailing whitespace removed.

‘Whitespace’ is defined according to the terms of the Unicode Derived
Core Property `White_Space`, which includes newlines.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#text-directionality-1)Text directionality

A string is a sequence of bytes. `end` in this context means the last
position of that byte string; for a left-to-right language like English or
Russian, this will be right side, and for right-to-left languages like
Arabic or Hebrew, this will be the left side.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-39)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let s = "\n Hello\tworld\t\n";
assert_eq!("\n Hello\tworld", s.trim_end());
```
Directionality:

```
let s = "  English  ";
assert!(Some('h') == s.trim_end().chars().rev().next());
let s = "  עברית  ";
assert!(Some('ת') == s.trim_end().chars().rev().next());
```
Returns a string slice with leading whitespace removed.

‘Whitespace’ is defined according to the terms of the Unicode Derived
Core Property `White_Space`.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#text-directionality-2)Text directionality

A string is a sequence of bytes. ‘Left’ in this context means the first
position of that byte string; for a language like Arabic or Hebrew
which are ‘right to left’ rather than ‘left to right’, this will be
the *right* side, not the left.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-40)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let s = " Hello\tworld\t";
assert_eq!("Hello\tworld\t", s.trim_left());
```
Directionality:

```
let s = "  English";
assert!(Some('E') == s.trim_left().chars().next());
let s = "  עברית";
assert!(Some('ע') == s.trim_left().chars().next());
```

assert_eq!("foo:bar".strip_prefix("bar"), None);
assert_eq!("foofoo".strip_prefix("foo"), Some("foo"));
```

`assert_eq!("1fooX".trim_right_matches(|c| c == '1' || c == 'X'), "1foo");`Parses this string slice into another type.

Because `parse` is so general, it can cause problems with type
inference. As such, `parse` is one of the few times you’ll see
the syntax affectionately known as the ‘turbofish’: `::<>`. This
helps the inference algorithm understand specifically which type
you’re trying to parse into.

`parse` can parse into any type that implements the [ FromStr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html) trait.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#errors)Errors

Will return [ Err](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html#associatedtype.Err) if it’s not possible to parse this string slice into
the desired type.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-49)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let four: u32 = "4".parse().unwrap();
assert_eq!(4, four);
```
Using the ‘turbofish’ instead of annotating `four`:

```
let four = "4".parse::<u32>();
assert_eq!(Ok(4), four);
```
Failing to parse:

```
let nope = "j".parse::<u32>();
assert!(nope.is_err());
```

`substr_range`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#2943)

#### pub fn [substr_range](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.substr_range)(&self, substr: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Range](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/range/struct.Range.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>>

`substr_range`)Returns the range that a substring points to.

Returns `None` if `substr` does not point within `self`.

Unlike [ str::find](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.find),

**this does not search through the string**. Instead, it uses pointer arithmetic to find where in the string

`substr` is derived from.This is useful for extending [ str::split](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split) and similar methods.

Note that this method may return false positives (typically either
`Some(0..0)` or `Some(self.len()..self.len())`) if `substr` is a
zero-length `str` that points at the beginning or end of another,
independent, `str`.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-58)Examples

```
#![feature(substr_range)]
let data = "a, b, b, a";
let mut iter = data.split(", ").map(|s| data.substr_range(s).unwrap());
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(0..1));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(3..4));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(6..7));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(9..10));
```
Returns the same string as a string slice `&str`.

This method is redundant when used directly on `&str`, but
it helps dereferencing other string-like types to string slices,
for example references to `Box<str>` or `Arc<str>`.

Replaces all matches of a pattern with another string.

`replace` creates a new [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), and copies the data from this string slice into it.
While doing so, it attempts to find matches of a pattern. If it finds any, it
replaces them with the replacement string slice.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-59)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let s = "this is old";
assert_eq!("this is new", s.replace("old", "new"));
assert_eq!("than an old", s.replace("is", "an"));
```
When the pattern doesn’t match, it returns this string slice as [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html):

```
let s = "this is old";
assert_eq!(s, s.replace("cookie monster", "little lamb"));
```
Replaces first N matches of a pattern with another string.

`replacen` creates a new [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), and copies the data from this string slice into it.
While doing so, it attempts to find matches of a pattern. If it finds any, it
replaces them with the replacement string slice at most

`count` times.[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-60)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let s = "foo foo 123 foo";
assert_eq!("new new 123 foo", s.replacen("foo", "new", 2));
assert_eq!("faa fao 123 foo", s.replacen('o', "a", 3));
assert_eq!("foo foo new23 foo", s.replacen(char::is_numeric, "new", 1));
```
When the pattern doesn’t match, it returns this string slice as [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html):

```
let s = "this is old";
assert_eq!(s, s.replacen("cookie monster", "little lamb", 10));
```
1.2.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#383)#### pub fn [to_lowercase](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.to_lowercase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#383)

#### pub fn [to_lowercase](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.to_lowercase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

Returns the lowercase equivalent of this string slice, as a new [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html).

‘Lowercase’ is defined according to the terms of the Unicode Derived Core Property
`Lowercase`.

Since some characters can expand into multiple characters when changing
the case, this function returns a [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html) instead of modifying the
parameter in-place.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-61)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let s = "HELLO";
assert_eq!("hello", s.to_lowercase());
```
A tricky example, with sigma:

```
let sigma = "Σ";
assert_eq!("σ", sigma.to_lowercase());
// but at the end of a word, it's ς, not σ:
let odysseus = "ὈΔΥΣΣΕΎΣ";
assert_eq!("ὀδυσσεύς", odysseus.to_lowercase());
```
Languages without case are not changed:

```
let new_year = "农历新年";
assert_eq!(new_year, new_year.to_lowercase());
```
1.2.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#470)#### pub fn [to_uppercase](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.to_uppercase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#470)

#### pub fn [to_uppercase](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.to_uppercase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

Returns the uppercase equivalent of this string slice, as a new [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html).

‘Uppercase’ is defined according to the terms of the Unicode Derived Core Property
`Uppercase`.

Since some characters can expand into multiple characters when changing
the case, this function returns a [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html) instead of modifying the
parameter in-place.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-62)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let s = "hello";
assert_eq!("HELLO", s.to_uppercase());
```
Scripts without case are not changed:

```
let new_year = "农历新年";
assert_eq!(new_year, new_year.to_uppercase());
```
One character can become multiple:

```
let s = "tschüß";
assert_eq!("TSCHÜSS", s.to_uppercase());
```
1.23.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#564)#### pub fn [to_ascii_uppercase](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.to_ascii_uppercase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#564)

#### pub fn [to_ascii_uppercase](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.to_ascii_uppercase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

Returns a copy of this string where each character is mapped to its ASCII upper case equivalent.

ASCII letters ‘a’ to ‘z’ are mapped to ‘A’ to ‘Z’, but non-ASCII letters are unchanged.

To uppercase the value in-place, use [ make_ascii_uppercase](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.make_ascii_uppercase).

To uppercase ASCII characters in addition to non-ASCII characters, use
[ to_uppercase](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.to_uppercase).

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-64)Examples

```
let s = "Grüße, Jürgen ❤";
assert_eq!("GRüßE, JüRGEN ❤", s.to_ascii_uppercase());
```
1.23.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#596)#### pub fn [to_ascii_lowercase](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.to_ascii_lowercase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#596)

#### pub fn [to_ascii_lowercase](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.to_ascii_lowercase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

Returns a copy of this string where each character is mapped to its ASCII lower case equivalent.

ASCII letters ‘A’ to ‘Z’ are mapped to ‘a’ to ‘z’, but non-ASCII letters are unchanged.

To lowercase the value in-place, use [ make_ascii_lowercase](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.make_ascii_lowercase).

To lowercase ASCII characters in addition to non-ASCII characters, use
[ to_lowercase](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#method.to_lowercase).

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#examples-65)Examples

```
let s = "Grüße, Jürgen ❤";
assert_eq!("grüße, jürgen ❤", s.to_ascii_lowercase());
```

# fixture in testing - Rust

Source: https://rustdoc.swc.rs/testing/attr.fixture.html

`#[fixture]`## Expand description

Create tests from files.

**NOTE: Path should be relative to the directory of  Cargo.toml file**.
This is limitation of current proc macro api.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#why)Why

If you create test dynamically, running a specific test become very cumbersome.

For example, if you use `test` crate with nightly, you can’t use `cargo test foo` to run tests with name containing `foo`. Instead, you have to implement
your own ignoring logic

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#usage)Usage

If you want to load all typescript files from `pass`

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#return-value)Return value

The function is allowed to return `Result` on error. If it’s the case

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#ignoring-a-test)Ignoring a test

If the path to the file contains a component starts with `.` (dot), it will
be ignore. This convention is widely used in many projects (including other
languages), as a file or a directory starting with `.` means hidden file in
unix system.

Note that they are added as a test `#[ignore]`, so you can use
`cargo test -- --ignored` or `cargo test -- --include-ignored` to run those
tests.

[§](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#roadmap)Roadmap

- Support async function

---

# diff_json_value in testing::json - Rust

Source: https://rustdoc.swc.rs/testing/json/fn.diff_json_value.html

```
pub fn diff_json_value(
    a: &mut
```
[Value](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.140/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html),
    b: &mut [Value](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.140/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html),
    normalize: &mut dyn [FnMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnMut.html)(&[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), &mut [Value](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.140/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html)),
) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)## Expand description

Remove common properties, recursively. You can optionally normalize more by passing a closure.

Closure takes `(key, value)`.

Returns `true` if `actual` and `expected` are equal.

# json.rs - source

Source: https://rustdoc.swc.rs/src/testing/json.rs.html

[1](#1)use serde_json::Value;
[2](#2)
[3](#3)fn normalize_value_recursively(v: &mut Value, normalize: &mut dyn FnMut(&str, &mut Value)) {
[4](#4)    match v {
[5](#5)        Value::Array(arr) => {
[6](#6)            for v in arr {
[7](#7)                normalize_value_recursively(v, normalize);
[8](#8)            }
[9](#9)        }
[10](#10)
[11](#11)        Value::Object(obj) => {
[12](#12)            for (k, v) in obj.iter_mut() {
[13](#13)                normalize(k, v);
[14](#14)            }
[15](#15)
[16](#16)            for (_, v) in obj.iter_mut() {
[17](#17)                normalize_value_recursively(v, normalize);
[18](#18)            }
[19](#19)        }
[20](#20)
[21](#21)        _ => {}
[22](#22)    }
[23](#23)}
[24](#24)
[25](#25)pub fn diff_json_value(
[32](#32)    a: &mut Value,
[33](#33)    b: &mut Value,
[34](#34)    normalize: &mut dyn FnMut(&str, &mut Value),
[35](#35)) -> bool {
[36](#36)    normalize_value_recursively(a, normalize);
[37](#37)    normalize_value_recursively(b, normalize);
[38](#38)
[39](#39)    remove_common(a, b)
[40](#40)}
[41](#41)
[42](#42)fn remove_common(a: &mut Value, b: &mut Value) -> bool {
[43](#43)    if *a == *b {
[44](#44)        return true;
[45](#45)    }
[46](#46)
[47](#47)    match (&mut *a, &mut *b) {
[48](#48)        (Value::Object(a), Value::Object(b)) => {
[49](#49)            if a.is_empty() && b.is_empty() {
[50](#50)                return true;
[51](#51)            }
[52](#52)
[53](#53)            a.retain(|key, a_v| {
[54](#54)                if let Some(b_v) = b.get_mut(key) {
[55](#55)                    if remove_common(a_v, b_v) {
[56](#56)                        b.remove(key);
[58](#58)                        return false;
[59](#59)                    }
[60](#60)                } else {
[61](#61)                    if a_v == &Value::Null {
[63](#63)                        return false;
[64](#64)                    }
[65](#65)                }
[66](#66)
[67](#67)                true
[69](#69)            });
[70](#70)            b.retain(|key, b_v| {
[71](#71)                if b_v == &Value::Null && !a.contains_key(key) {
[73](#73)                    return false;
[74](#74)                }
[75](#75)
[76](#76)                true
[79](#79)            });
[80](#80)        }
[81](#81)
[82](#82)        (Value::Array(a), Value::Array(b)) => {
[83](#83)            if a.len() == b.len() {
[84](#84)                for (a_v, b_v) in a.iter_mut().zip(b.iter_mut()) {
[85](#85)                    remove_common(a_v, b_v);
[86](#86)                }
[87](#87)            }
[88](#88)        }
[89](#89)
[90](#90)        _ => {}
[91](#91)    }
[92](#92)
[93](#93)    false
[94](#94)}

---

[56](#56)fn normalize_input(input: String, skip_last_newline: bool) -> String {
[57](#57)    let manifest_dirs = [
[58](#58)        adjust_canonicalization(paths::manifest_dir()),
[59](#59)        paths::manifest_dir().to_string_lossy().to_string(),
[60](#60)    ]
[61](#61)    .into_iter()
[62](#62)    .flat_map(|dir| [dir.replace('\\', "\\\\"), dir.replace('\\', "/"), dir])
[63](#63)    .collect::<Vec<_>>();
[64](#64)
[65](#65)    let input = input.replace("\r\n", "\n");
[66](#66)
[67](#67)    let mut buf = String::new();
[68](#68)
[69](#69)    for line in input.lines() {
[70](#70)        if manifest_dirs.iter().any(|dir| line.contains(&**dir)) {
[71](#71)            let mut s = line.to_string();
[72](#72)
[73](#73)            for dir in &manifest_dirs {
[74](#74)                s = s.replace(&**dir, "$DIR");
[75](#75)            }
[76](#76)            s = s.replace("\\\\", "\\").replace('\\', "/");
[77](#77)            let s = if cfg!(target_os = "windows") {
[78](#78)                s.replace("//?/$DIR", "$DIR").replace("/?/$DIR", "$DIR")
[79](#79)            } else {
[80](#80)                s
[81](#81)            };
[82](#82)            buf.push_str(&s)
[83](#83)        } else {
[84](#84)            buf.push_str(line);
[85](#85)        }
[86](#86)
[87](#87)        buf.push('\n');
[88](#88)    }
[89](#89)
[90](#90)    if skip_last_newline && !matches!(input.chars().last(), Some('\n')) {
[91](#91)        buf.truncate(buf.len() - 1);
[92](#92)    }
[93](#93)
[94](#94)    buf
[95](#95)}

[106](#106)    pub fn compare_json_to_file<T>(actual: &T, path: &Path)
[107](#107)    where
[108](#108)        T: Serialize,
[109](#109)    {
[110](#110)        let actual_value =
[111](#111)            serde_json::to_value(actual).expect("failed to serialize the actual value to json");
[112](#112)
[113](#113)        if let Ok(expected) = fs::read_to_string(path) {
[114](#114)            let expected_value = serde_json::from_str::<serde_json::Value>(&expected)
[115](#115)                .expect("failed to deserialize the expected value from json");
[116](#116)
[117](#117)            if expected_value == actual_value {
[118](#118)                return;
[119](#119)            }
[120](#120)        }
[121](#121)
[122](#122)        let actual_json_string = serde_json::to_string_pretty(&actual_value)
[123](#123)            .expect("failed to serialize the actual value to json");
[124](#124)
[125](#125)        let _ = NormalizedOutput::from(actual_json_string).compare_to_file(path);
[126](#126)    }
[127](#127)
[128](#128)    pub fn compare_to_file<P>(self, path: P) -> Result<(), Diff>
[132](#132)    where
[133](#133)        P: AsRef<Path>,
[134](#134)    {
[135](#135)        let path = path.as_ref();
[136](#136)        let path = path.canonicalize().unwrap_or_else(|err| {
[137](#137)            debug!(
[138](#138)                "compare_to_file: failed to canonicalize outfile path `{}`: {:?}",
[139](#139)                path.display(),
[140](#140)                err
[141](#141)            );
[142](#142)            path.to_path_buf()
[143](#143)        });
[144](#144)
[145](#145)        let expected: NormalizedOutput = NormalizedOutput(
[146](#146)            File::open(&path)
[147](#147)                .map(|mut file| {
[148](#148)                    let mut buf = String::new();
[149](#149)                    file.read_to_string(&mut buf).unwrap();
[150](#150)                    buf
[151](#151)                })
[152](#152)                .unwrap_or_else(|_| {
[153](#153)                    String::new()
[155](#155)                })
[156](#156)                .replace("\r\n", "\n"),
[157](#157)        );
[158](#158)
[159](#159)        if expected == self {
[160](#160)            return Ok(());
[161](#161)        }
[162](#162)
[163](#163)        debug!("Comparing output to {}", path.display());
[164](#164)        create_dir_all(path.parent().unwrap()).expect("failed to run `mkdir -p`");
[165](#165)
[166](#166)        let update = std::env::var("UPDATE").unwrap_or_default() == "1";
[167](#167)        if update {
[168](#168)            crate::write_to_file(&path, &self.0);
[169](#169)
[170](#170)            debug!("Updating file {}", path.display());
[171](#171)            return Ok(());
[172](#172)        }
[173](#173)
[174](#174)        if !update && self.0.lines().count() <= 5 {
[175](#175)            assert_eq!(expected, self, "Actual:\n{self}");
[176](#176)        }
[177](#177)
[178](#178)        let diff = Diff {
[179](#179)            expected,
[180](#180)            actual: self,
[181](#181)        };
[182](#182)
[183](#183)        if env::var("DIFF").unwrap_or_default() == "0" {
[184](#184)            assert_eq!(diff.expected, diff.actual, "Actual:\n{}", diff.actual);
[185](#185)        } else {
[186](#186)            pretty_assertions::assert_eq!(diff.expected, diff.actual, "Actual:\n{}", diff.actual);
[187](#187)        }
[188](#188)
[189](#189)        Err(diff)
[191](#191)    }

[226](#226)fn adjust_canonicalization<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P) -> String {
[227](#227)    const VERBATIM_PREFIX: &str = r#"\\?\"#;
[228](#228)    let p = p.as_ref().display().to_string();
[229](#229)    if let Some(stripped) = p.strip_prefix(VERBATIM_PREFIX) {
[230](#230)        stripped.to_string()
[231](#231)    } else {
[232](#232)        p

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://rustdoc.swc.rs/src/testing_macros/lib.rs.html

# testing_macros/lib.rs

[1](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#1)use proc_macro::TokenStream;
[2](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#2)use quote::{quote, ToTokens};
[3](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#3)use syn::ItemFn;
[4](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#4)
[5](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#5)mod fixture;
[6](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#6)
[7](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#7)/// Create tests from files.
[8](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#8)///
[9](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#9)/// **NOTE: Path should be relative to the directory of `Cargo.toml` file**.
[10](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#10)/// This is limitation of current proc macro api.
[11](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#11)///
[12](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#12)/// # Why
[13](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#13)///
[14](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#14)/// If you create test dynamically, running a specific test become very
[15](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#15)/// cumbersome.
[16](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#16)///
[17](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#17)/// For example, if you use `test` crate with nightly, you can't use `cargo test
[18](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#18)/// foo` to run tests with name containing `foo`. Instead, you have to implement
[19](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#19)/// your own ignoring logic
[20](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#20)///
[21](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#21)///
[22](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#22)/// # Usage
[23](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#23)///
[24](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#24)/// If you want to load all typescript files from `pass`
[25](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#25)///
[26](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#26)/// ```rust,ignore
[27](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#27)///
[28](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#28)/// #[fixture("pass/**/*.{ts,tsx}")]
[29](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#29)/// fn pass(file: PathBuf) {
[30](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#30)///     // test by reading file
[31](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#31)/// }
[32](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#32)/// ```
[33](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#33)///
[34](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#34)/// # Return value
[35](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#35)///
[36](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#36)/// The function is allowed to return `Result` on error. If it's the case
[37](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#37)///
[38](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#38)///
[39](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#39)/// ## Ignoring a test
[40](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#40)///
[41](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#41)/// If the path to the file contains a component starts with `.` (dot), it will
[42](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#42)/// be ignore. This convention is widely used in many projects (including other
[43](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#43)/// languages), as a file or a directory starting with `.` means hidden file in
[44](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#44)/// unix system.
[45](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#45)///
[46](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#46)/// Note that they are added as a test `#[ignore]`, so you can use
[47](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#47)/// `cargo test -- --ignored` or `cargo test -- --include-ignored` to run those
[48](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#48)/// tests.
[49](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#49)///
[50](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#50)///
[51](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#51)/// # Roadmap
[52](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#52)///
[53](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#53)/// - Support async function
[54](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#54)#[proc_macro_attribute]
[55](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#55)pub fn fixture(attr: TokenStream, item: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
[56](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#56)    let item: ItemFn = syn::parse(item).expect("failed to parse input as a function item");
[57](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#57)
[58](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#58)    if cfg!(feature = "rust-analyzer") {
[59](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#59)        return quote!(
[60](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#60)            #[allow(unused)]
[61](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#61)            #item
[62](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#62)        )
[63](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#63)        .into();
[64](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#64)    }
[65](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#65)
[66](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#66)    let config: self::fixture::Config =
[67](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#67)        syn::parse(attr).expect("failed to parse input passed to #[fixture]");
[68](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#68)
[69](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#69)    let cases = self::fixture::expand(&item.sig.ident, config).unwrap();
[70](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#70)
[71](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#71)    let mut output = proc_macro2::TokenStream::new();
[72](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#72)
[73](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#73)    for case in cases {
[74](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#74)        case.to_tokens(&mut output);
[75](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#75)    }
[76](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#76)
[77](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#77)    item.to_tokens(&mut output);
[78](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#78)
[79](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#79)    output.into()
[80](https://rustdoc.swc.rs#80)}
